hello.note: Oi (oy), hi, is what most Brazilians say, to almost anyone

how-are-you.note: Literally "all good?", the everyday greeting. The answer is often the same words: Tudo bem!

im-well.note: A man says obrigado and a woman obrigada

good-morning.note: Until about noon. Then boa tarde (BOH-ah TAR-jee), and after dark boa noite

good-night.note: Good evening as well as good night, both meeting and parting

goodbye.note: From Italian ciao, and the usual goodbye. Até logo (ah-TEH LOH-goo), see you later, is a little more formal

thank-you.note: Literally "obliged". A man says obrigado and a woman obrigada, whoever they thank

youre-welcome.note: Also heard: imagina (ee-mah-JEE-nah), don't mention it

yes.note: Brazilians often answer by repeating the verb instead: Tem? Tem! (do you have it? I have)

no.note: A nasal sound, like "now" said through the nose. Não, obrigado is no, thank you

excuse-me.note: Com licença, with your permission, to get past or get attention. Desculpe is sorry

my-name.note: The audio uses Peter as the example name

your-name.note: Polite and the same for anyone. Friends say Como você se chama?

where-from.note: Você is the everyday you in Brazil. To an older person, o senhor (to a man) or a senhora (to a woman) is more respectful

its-beautiful.note: For a place or a view. Que lindo! means how beautiful!

dont-understand.note: Literally "I didn't understand", the way Brazilians say it

speak-slowly.text: Pode falar mais devagar, por favor?
speak-slowly.say: POH-jee fah-LAR myce jee-vah-GAR, poor fah-VOR

repeat.note: Pode...? (POH-jee), can you...?, starts a polite request

speak-english.note: Outside the tourist areas, few people speak English, so a little Portuguese goes a long way

six.note: In phone numbers Brazilians say meia (MAY-ah), half a dozen, so it isn't confused with três

hundred.note: Cento (SEN-too) when more follows: cento e dez is 110

thousand.note: Prices are in reais (hay-ICE), written R$: mil reais is R$ 1.000

hundred-thousand.note: Written 100.000: Brazil marks thousands with a dot and decimals with a comma

how-much.note: Point and say Quanto custa isso? (EE-soo), how much is this?

would-like.note: Literally "I wanted...", the polite way to order, the same for a man or a woman. The audio uses um café (oong kah-FEH), a coffee, as the example

i-want.note: More direct than eu queria. Add por favor. The audio uses este (ES-chee), this one, as the example

do-you-have.note: Literally "is there...?", the everyday way to ask in a shop. The audio uses água (AH-gwah), water, as the example

just-looking.note: The same for a man or a woman

too-expensive.note: Often shortened to tá caro (TAH KAH-roo)

discount.note: Paying cash, à vista (ah VEES-tah), often gets a discount in small shops and markets

card.note: Cards are taken almost everywhere. Many people pay by Pix, an instant bank transfer, which visitors usually can't use

bill.note: A 10% service charge is usually added to the bill

checkout-time.note: Brazilians use the English word, said their way

breakfast.text: O café da manhã está incluído?
breakfast.say: oo kah-FEH dah mahn-YAHN es-TAH een-kloo-EE-doo
breakfast.note: Brazilian hotel breakfasts are famously generous, with fruit, cakes and pão de queijo, cheese bread

wifi.text: Qual é a senha do Wi-Fi?
wifi.say: kwah-OO EH ah SEN-yah doo wy-FY

toilet.note: Onde fica...? (OHN-jee FEE-kah) asks where anything is

taxi.text: Pode chamar um táxi para mim?
taxi.say: POH-jee shah-MAR oong TAHK-see PAH-rah meen
taxi.note: Ride apps like Uber and 99 are very widely used

train.note: Brazil has few passenger trains. City metros are the metrô (meh-TROH)

bus.note: The same word for one bus or many

bus-station.note: The long-distance bus station. Brazil travels by bus, and the coaches are comfortable. A city bus stop is a ponto de ônibus

train-station.note: A metro station is an estação de metrô

where-train-station.text: Onde fica a estação de trem?
where-train-station.say: OHN-jee FEE-kah ah es-tah-SOWN jee trayn

which-train.note: Para (PAH-rah, often just prah) means to. The audio uses Campinas as the example

buy-ticket.note: A passagem is a ticket for a journey. For the metro or a show it is a bilhete or ingresso

two-tickets.note: The audio uses Paraty, a favourite coastal town, as the example
two-tickets.spoken: Duas passagens para Paraty, por favor

trip-length.text: Quanto tempo leva a viagem até...?
trip-length.say: KWAHN-too TEM-poo LEH-vah ah vee-AH-zhayn ah-TEH ...
trip-length.note: The audio uses Paraty as the example
trip-length.spoken: Quanto tempo leva a viagem até Paraty?
trip-length.filled: Quanto tempo leva a viagem até ⟦Paraty⟧?

delicious.note: Brazilians often say Que gostoso! (kee gohs-TOH-zoo) or Uma delícia!

allergic.note: Add the food: frutos do mar (FROO-toos doo MAR) seafood, amendoim (ah-men-doh-EEN) peanuts, ovo (OH-voo) eggs. The audio uses seafood
allergic.spoken: Sou alérgico a frutos do mar

female.spoken: Sou alérgica a frutos do mar

love-dish.note: Literally "I loved this dish", the same for a man or a woman

what-called.note: Point at the dish or item

table-for-two.text: Uma mesa para dois, por favor
table-for-two.say: OO-mah MEH-zah PAH-rah doyss, poor fah-VOR
table-for-two.note: For more people: para três, 3, or para quatro, 4

menu.note: Many restaurants show the menu by QR code. A per-kilo buffet, comida a quilo, is a cheap, good lunch

beer.note: Beer comes very cold, often a big bottle to share. Bem gelada (bayn zheh-LAH-dah) means ice-cold

coffee.note: A small, strong black coffee, a cafezinho, is offered everywhere. With milk: café com leite

water.note: Com gás (kohn GAHS) sparkling, sem gás (sayn GAHS) still. Drink bottled water

sugar.note: Juices often come sweetened. Sem açúcar (sayn ah-SOO-kar) means without sugar

hot.note: Hot, and hot weather. Spicy is picante or apimentado

cold.note: Cold weather and cold food. A cold drink is gelado (zheh-LAH-doo)

cheers.note: Literally "health". Also tim-tim! (cheen-CHEEN), the clink of glasses

help.note: Shout it. The police are on 190

need-doctor.note: The same for a man or a woman. For an ambulance (SAMU), call 192

pharmacy.note: Big chains like Drogasil and Droga Raia are everywhere, and many are open 24 hours
